issues.legal_issue: A surplus from selling an asset acquired and held as an investment is a capital realisation rather than trading income when the circumstances show that the asset was not acquired for trade.
material_facts: The assessee was a landholder and the transactions were outside the ordinary course of any business he carried on.
During wartime uncertainty, he converted his shareholdings and additional funds into gold, which he kept in family vaults for nearly four years.
Although gold prices rose substantially before the sale, he did not sell it during that rise and sold almost all of it in a short period after confidence returned.
The sale proceeds were used to acquire other investments.
issues.conclusion: The surpluses from the gold sales were capital realisations, not profits from an adventure in the nature of trade, and were not taxable as trading income.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 4(3)(vii) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, a surplus from realising an investment is not taxable as a trading profit unless the transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade. Whether it is such an adventure depends on the transaction's character assessed from all the facts and the assessee's conduct; the fact that an asset might later be sold at an enhanced price is not by itself enough. The court relied on the principles in Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. C.I.T. and Liquidators of Pursa Ltd. v. C.I.T.

predicates.tax_assessment_of_surplus_from_asset_sal: A tax assessment treats a surplus from selling an asset as income or profit.
predicates.asset_acquired_as_shelter_during_wartime: The holder converted investments into the asset in response to wartime uncertainty.
predicates.asset_held_for_years_without_sale_as_pri: The holder kept the asset for years without selling it while its price rose substantially.
predicates.most_asset_sold_together_after_confidenc: The holder sold nearly all of the asset together after confidence returned.

issues.definition: When a tax assessment concerns a surplus from an asset sale and the asset was acquired as a shelter during wartime uncertainty, held through a substantial price rise, and mostly sold together after confidence returned, the surplus is a capital realisation rather than taxable trade profit.

issues.legal_issue: A profit from selling shares acquired as part of a plan to obtain control of a company is a capital accretion when the shares were not acquired for dealing in them.
material_facts: The assessee acquired shares in a company while seeking to obtain control of its management through a majority holding.
The market purchases and the proposed acquisition of shares representing unissued capital were parts of the same plan.
The plan failed, and the assessee sold nearly all the shares acquired in the market, retaining only a small number.
issues.conclusion: The profit on the sale of the shares was on capital account and was not a trading profit.
issues.legal_principle: The character of a share transaction depends on whether the shares were held as stock-in-trade or as an investment. A profit from shares acquired to obtain control of a company, rather than to deal in them, is on capital account. The court relied on Kishan Prasad & Co. Ltd. v. C.I.T. and C.I.T. v. National Finance Ltd.

predicates.tax_assessment_of_share_sale_profit: A tax assessment treats a profit from selling shares as trading income.
predicates.shares_acquired_as_part_of_company_contr: The holder acquired shares as part of a plan to obtain control of a company's management.
predicates.market_purchases_and_proposed_unissued_s: The holder's market purchases and proposed acquisition of unissued shares were components of the same control plan.
predicates.control_plan_failed_and_most_shares_were: The plan to obtain control failed, and the holder sold nearly all the shares acquired.

issues.definition: When a share-sale profit is assessed as trading income but the shares were acquired as part of a control plan, the market purchases and proposed acquisition of unissued shares formed one plan, and the failed plan was followed by the sale of most of the shares, the profit is capital rather than trading income.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade is a mixed question of fact and law, so a High Court hearing a tax reference may review the Tribunal's conclusion if it misdirected itself in law.
material_facts: The appeals arose from tax references concerning whether transactions in assets were investment realisations or adventures in the nature of trade.
The Tribunal treated its conclusions about the transactions as factual, and the High Court declined to interfere on the ground that the findings were supported by evidence.
The Supreme Court concluded that the Tribunal had misapplied the law to the facts and that the High Court could have reviewed its findings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to treat the Tribunal's conclusions as unreviewable findings of pure fact; it could review the mixed question where the Tribunal misdirected itself in law.
issues.legal_principle: The expression “adventure in the nature of trade” entails legal elements that give a transaction the character of trade or business. The ultimate conclusion drawn by applying those legal elements to established facts is a mixed question of fact and law and is reviewable in a tax reference where the Tribunal misdirects itself in law. The court relied on Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. C.I.T., Liquidators of Pursa Ltd. v. C.I.T., and Sree Meenakshi Mills Ltd. v. C.I.T.

predicates.tax_reference_on_trade_character_of_tran: A High Court is hearing a tax reference about whether transactions were investments or adventures in the nature of trade.
predicates.tribunal_conclusion_applies_legal_test_t: The Tribunal's conclusion applies a legal test to facts it has found.
predicates.tribunal_misdirected_itself_in_law: The Tribunal misapplied or misunderstood the law when reaching its conclusion.

issues.definition: In a tax reference concerning the trade character of transactions, where the Tribunal applied a legal test to found facts but misdirected itself in law, the High Court may review the mixed question.

issues.legal_issue: A Tribunal is not barred from reaching a different conclusion about the character of transactions in a later assessment when it considers the assessee's conduct over a more complete period and that conduct supports a different conclusion.
material_facts: In earlier assessments, the Tribunal had treated transactions in investments as changes from one investment to another rather than as trading.
In the later proceedings, the Tribunal considered the transactions over a longer period, including later purchases and sales.
The Supreme Court held that this broader view could permit a different conclusion if the assessee's acts and conduct as a whole pointed to it.
issues.conclusion: There was no bar to the Tribunal reaching a different conclusion from the earlier assessments on the basis of the transactions and conduct considered over the whole period.
issues.legal_principle: A Tribunal may reach a different conclusion in a later assessment when it has a more comprehensive picture of the transactions and the assessee's conduct over the relevant period points to a different result. The difference in conclusion is not barred merely because an earlier Tribunal reached a different conclusion on earlier assessments.

predicates.later_tax_assessment_considers_transacti: A later tax assessment considers whether a series of transactions was investment or trade.
predicates.earlier_assessments_reached_a_different_: Earlier assessments reached a different conclusion about the character of the transactions.
predicates.later_tribunal_considers_a_more_comprehe: The Tribunal in the later proceedings considers transactions and conduct over a more comprehensive period.

issues.definition: When a later assessment revisits the character of transactions after earlier assessments reached a different conclusion, the Tribunal is not barred from reaching a different conclusion if it considers a more comprehensive period of conduct.
